content: 1. Food system policies and programs should be designed to monitor and address potential trade-offs effectively. 2. Agro-biodiversity should be supported as a natural control measure to reduce the dependency on chemical pesticides and herbicides. 3. Quarantine capabilities, sentinel monitoring programs, and strategies for identifying and managing pests, weeds, and disease threats must be enhanced to counteract pathogens and pests that are likely to thrive due to climate change. 4. Soil health management can be improved through the use of cover crops, legumes, composting, and agroforestry systems. 5. Land clearing should be curbed, and measures should be implemented to prevent further land degradation and loss of soil fertility, which will also enhance productivity and resilience to climate change. 6. Initiatives that integrate traditional and modern farming practices should be supported, as they promote biodiversity, demonstrate climate-smart and nutrition-smart practices, and improve soil health, pest and disease management, and water storage and harvesting. 7. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and Integrated Vector Management (IVM) are alternative approaches that reduce reliance on pesticides. These methods are based on a thorough understanding of local ecosystems and require decentralized decision-making at the local level, supported by regular field observations and clear criteria. 8. Sustainable production and consumption of local foods, including neglected and underutilized species with high nutritional value, should be promoted. 9. Awareness and capacity-building efforts should focus on the threats posed to imported grain-based foods and the climate resilience and nutritional benefits of traditional food crops, ensuring this information reaches rural communities. 10. Opportunities to support traditional food cultures should be identified, not only as a health-promoting measure but also to strengthen community resilience, livelihoods, and well-being. 11. Ecosystem-based approaches should be promoted to enhance understanding of the importance of good ecosystem management at the farmer and community levels, supporting resilience in landscapes and seascapes. 12. Vegetation in catchments should be managed and restored to sustain coastal fish production, reduce sediment and nutrient runoff, and protect ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrass habitats, and wetlands. 13. Measures to improve the resilience of freshwater and coastal fisheries to climate change and biodiversity loss should include pollution control, waste management, and the prohibition of activities that damage coral reefs, wetlands, and mangroves. 14. Communities should be empowered to protect fish habitats while using them sustainably, combining traditional approaches with government regulations. 15. Post-harvest fish processing methods, such as smoke curing, salting, and drying, should be improved to reduce waste, extend shelf life, and create opportunities for trade with inland communities. 16. School feeding programs should incorporate locally produced, high-nutritional-value foods, including neglected and underutilized species, to promote healthy food environments for school-aged children. 17. Food and beverage guidelines for schools should be established, and the marketing and labeling of unhealthy foods and beverages targeting children should be regulated. 18. Education on the nutritional value of locally sourced foods, including neglected and underutilized species, should be promoted through school gardens and integration into school curricula. 19. Surveillance and monitoring systems should adopt a One Health approach to enable early detection of pathogens transmissible between humans, wildlife, and livestock. 20. Integrated food chain surveillance should be implemented to conduct risk analysis for foodborne diseases, and participatory approaches should be embedded in monitoring and evaluation efforts. 21. Policies, subsidies, and economic incentives should support the production of nutritious foods, including fruits, vegetables, pulses, and underutilized species, to achieve the full potential of nutrition-sensitive agriculture and biodiversity. 22. Sustainable and healthy diets should be promoted to reduce malnutrition, diet-related non-communicable diseases, and greenhouse gas emissions, while ensuring that both human health and the health of natural systems are enhanced. 23. Cross-sector analysis of co-benefits and potential trade-offs associated with policy decisions is necessary to ensure the successful implementation of sustainable and healthy diets. 24. Sustainable diets, as defined by the FAO, are those with low environmental impacts that contribute to food and nutrition security and healthy lives for present and future generations. They are protective of biodiversity and ecosystems, culturally acceptable, accessible, economically fair, and nutritionally adequate. 25. The United Nations has declared a Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016–2025) to end all forms of malnutrition and ensure universal access to healthier and more sustainable diets. WHO is co-leading the implementation of this initiative.
